summary: Fine-tuning makes sense when you need to reliably change a model's behavior, tone, or output format, teach it a narrow domain, or reduce latency/cost by distilling a large model's behavior into a smaller one. RAG is better when you need up-to-date or proprietary factual knowledge that changes frequently, while prompt engineering is the cheapest first step for most tasks. In practice, teams reach for fine-tuning only after prompting and RAG have hit a ceiling on consistency, format adherence, or cost.
when_to_fine_tune: Choose fine-tuning when you need consistent output structure, style, or classification behavior that prompting alone can't reliably enforce.
Use it to distill a large, expensive model into a smaller, cheaper one that matches quality on your specific task.
Prefer RAG over fine-tuning when the core challenge is injecting fresh or frequently-changing factual knowledge.
Fine-tune for deep domain adaptation (legal, medical, code) or instruction/RLHF alignment where you have hundreds to thousands of high-quality labeled examples.
